location: Picasso, Miro, Dali: Unbound exhibition at MFA, Boston, MA

rows.stop: Le Lézard aux plumes d’or (The Lizard with Golden Feathers)
rows.text: Joan Miró's "Le Lézard aux plumes d’or," created in 1971, is a vivid testament to the collaborative spirit that transformed the book into an art form. Published by Louis Broder, a visionary in the realm of limited edition art books, this piece features 40 color lithographs, printed on luxurious publisher’s vellum. The lithographs were expertly crafted by Mourlot Frères, renowned for their ability to capture intricate details in color and form. Broder's decision to commission Miró is significant as it epitomizes the interweaving of artistic vision and technical expertise, with the poet, artist, and Mourlot Frères working in concert to produce a seamless work of art. This particular work exemplifies how text and imagery coalesce to offer a glimpse into the surreal, where the titular lizard unfurls its golden feathers amid a fantastical landscape. It prompts us to ponder what other art forms reveal the unseen truths of our world.
rows.orientation: You are about to explore the Picasso, Miro, Dali: Unbound exhibition at the Museum of Fine Arts in Boston. The collection features three extraordinary works by Spanish artists showcased in the Lois B. and Michael K. Torf Gallery (Gallery 184). These pieces are not just art; they are livres d'artiste, artist's books that had no precedent and revolutionized the book as an art form. This deeply collaborative venture explores how images, words, and typography intersect, offering a rare glimpse into the transformative power of light and belief in art. Get ready to immerse yourself in "Le Lézard aux plumes d’or (The Lizard with Golden Feathers)," "Au Soleil du Plafond," and "Moses and Monotheism." At Le Lézard aux plumes d’or (The Lizard with Golden Feathers), ponder unseen truths through various art forms. In Moses and Monotheism, Dalí highlights the book's revolutionary potential through image, text, and materiality. Your first stop is Le Lézard aux plumes d’or (The Lizard with Golden Feathers). From this vantage point, the interplay of vibrant colors in its lithographs becomes strikingly evident, inviting a deeper look into the surreal fusion of text and image that defines this piece.

rows.text: Gris, a seminal figure in Cubism, worked on this project, crafting 11 lithographs that captured his distinct artistry before his untimely death in 1927 left the piece unfinished. Despite this, Reverdy's unwavering commitment ensured the project’s completion decades later. The lithographs, printed on Arches paper, allow viewers to witness the vibrant synthesis of Gris’s visual imagination and Reverdy’s evocative text. This work exemplifies the exhibition’s argument that the book can transcend its traditional form and become a unified art piece. The initial collection of the Museum sourced from the Athenæum's Art Gallery, now makes this rare work accessible to the public, typically reserved for archives. The gallery where these collaborative efforts are displayed bears the name of Torf, whose patronage supports the curation of such deeply intertwined visual and written artistry. Here, viewers encounter an exploration of artistic vision that speaks across the years, beckoning them to consider the intricate dance of light — both literal and metaphorical. This concept of illumination extends beyond the page, inviting reflections on spiritual and ideological enlightenment.
rows.orientation: This vantage aligns you with the intricate play between Reverdy’s poetic text and Gris’s lithographs — a dialog that transforms as light strikes the pages.

rows.text:
In 1974, Salvador Dalí crafted a set of ten illustrations to accompany Sigmund Freud’s provocative text, "Moses and Monotheism." Freud, a towering figure in psychoanalysis, penned this work in 1939, proposing that Moses was an Egyptian nobleman rather than a Hebrew slave. Dalí was captivated by Freud’s theories, which allowed him to fuse his surrealist vision with psychoanalytic concepts. Rendered in drypoints and lithographs on sheepskin, Dalí's illustrations bring Freud's arguments to visual life, creating an unsettling yet compelling dialogue between imagery and text. By integrating these elements, Dalí contributes to the exhibition's thesis in a significant way, highlighting the revolutionary potential of the book as an artwork where image, text, and materiality coalesce.

That's 3 stops — Au Soleil du Plafond showcases Torf's collaborative visual and written artistry and Le Lézard aux plumes d’or invites reflection on unseen truths in art. rows.orientation: As you stand here, position yourself to see how Salvador Dalí’s illustrations interact with Sigmund Freud’s text in "Moses and Monotheism." From this vantage point, you can appreciate the tactile quality of the sheepskin and the intricacies of the illustrations and text, which are designed to be experienced as a unified whole.
